title: Attention from first principles: queries, keys, values, masking, multi-head
tagline: Derive attention, compute its cost, and know exactly what every tensor shape is.
explain:
**Idea**: a soft, differentiable dictionary lookup. For each query, compare it with all keys, turn scores into weights with softmax, and return the weighted sum of values.

```math
\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\Big)V,\qquad Q=XW_Q,\;K=XW_K,\;V=XW_V
```

**Shapes** (batch $B$, length $n$, model dim $d$, heads $h$, head dim $d_k=d/h$): $X\in\mathbb R^{B\times n\times d}$; $Q,K,V\in\mathbb R^{B\times h\times n\times d_k}$; scores $QK^\top\in\mathbb R^{B\times h\times n\times n}$; output $B\times h\times n\times d_k\to$ concat $\to B\times n\times d\to W_O$.

**Why $1/\sqrt{d_k}$**: for $q,k$ with i.i.d. unit-variance entries $\mathrm{Var}(q^\top k)=d_k$; unscaled scores grow with $d_k$ and the softmax saturates to one-hot (gradient $\approx0$). Use the lab: turn scaling off and raise $d_k$.

**Mask $M$**: $0$ allowed, $-\infty$ blocked. **Causal mask** (decoder) blocks $j>i$; **padding mask** blocks pad tokens; **cross-attention** takes $Q$ from the decoder and $K,V$ from the encoder.

**Multi-head attention**: $h$ parallel attention functions in separate subspaces, concatenated and mixed by $W_O$. Different heads specialise (positional, syntactic, copy/induction, delimiter heads). Same cost as one big head but more expressive. **Parameter count** of an attention layer: $4d^2$ ($W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O$).

**Cost**: time $O(n^2d)$, memory $O(n^2)$ per head for the score matrix (this is what FlashAttention avoids materialising). FLOPs ≈ $4n^2d$ (QK$^\top$ and AV) + $8nd^2$ (projections).

**Properties**: permutation-equivariant (so position information must be injected), $O(1)$ path length between any two tokens, input-dependent mixing weights (unlike fixed conv kernels). **Induction heads** implement in-context copying ("…A B … A → B") and are linked to in-context learning.

**Attention is not an explanation**: attention weights are *not* guaranteed to reflect feature importance (Jain & Wallace 2019); use gradient/attribution/intervention methods for interpretability.
tradeoffs: Full attention is the most expressive; the $n^2$ cost forces windowed/sparse/linear/state-space alternatives for long sequences.
More heads = more diversity but smaller $d_k$ per head; GQA/MQA share K,V across heads to cut the KV cache.
pitfalls: Forgetting the causal mask (information leak ⇒ implausibly low loss).
Mask added after softmax instead of before.
fp16 softmax overflow with large logits (compute in fp32).
Interpreting attention weights as causal explanations.
interview: Derive why we divide by sqrt(d_k).
What are the shapes at every step of multi-head attention?
What is the memory complexity and how does FlashAttention avoid it?
use: Understanding/writing any transformer; computing parameter and FLOP budgets in a paper.
avoid: Do not claim 'attention shows what the model looks at' without causal evidence.

qa.q: Why multiple heads instead of one head of dimension d?
qa.a: Each head attends over a different learned subspace, so the model can represent several different relations at the same position simultaneously; a single softmax distribution must average them into one pattern. The cost is identical because $h\cdot d_k=d$.

deep.title: Backward pass of softmax-attention
deep.body: With $S=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$, $P=\mathrm{softmax}(S)$, $O=PV$: $dV=P^\top dO$, $dP=dO\,V^\top$, $dS_{i\cdot}=P_{i\cdot}\odot(dP_{i\cdot}-\langle dP_{i\cdot},P_{i\cdot}\rangle)$, $dQ=dS\,K/\sqrt{d_k}$, $dK=dS^\top Q/\sqrt{d_k}$. FlashAttention recomputes $P$ block-wise in the backward pass instead of storing the $n\times n$ matrix.

title: The full transformer: block anatomy, positional encodings, parameter and FLOP counts
tagline: Everything inside a GPT/BERT/T5 block, with formulas you can compute on paper.
explain:
**Decoder-only block (pre-norm, LLaMA-style)**:

```math
x\leftarrow x+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x)),\qquad x\leftarrow x+\mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x)),\qquad \mathrm{FFN}(x)=W_2\big(\mathrm{SiLU}(W_1x)\odot W_3x\big)
```

Stack $L$ blocks between a token embedding (and tied or untied output head) and a final norm; logits $=h\,E^\top$ (weight tying shares the embedding and unembedding).

**Parameter counts** (per block, ignoring norms/biases): attention $4d^2$; FFN with hidden size $d_{ff}$: standard $2d\,d_{ff}$ ($d_{ff}=4d\Rightarrow8d^2$) or SwiGLU $3d\,d_{ff}$ ($d_{ff}\approx\frac83d\Rightarrow8d^2$). So **≈ $12d^2$ per block**, total $N\approx12Ld^2+Vd$. Example: $d=4096,L=32$ → $12\cdot32\cdot4096^2\approx6.4$B + embeddings ≈ 7B.

**FLOPs**: a forward pass costs ≈ $2N$ per token (each parameter used in one multiply-add) plus the attention term $\approx2Lnd$ per token; **training ≈ $6N$ per token** (forward $2N$ + backward $4N$). This is where the $C\approx6ND$ rule comes from.

**Positional information** (attention is permutation-equivariant):
- **Sinusoidal** (original): $PE_{pos,2i}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})$, $PE_{pos,2i+1}=\cos(\cdot)$ - fixed, extrapolates weakly.
- **Learned absolute** embeddings (GPT-2, BERT): fixed max length.
- **Relative** biases (T5) and **ALiBi**: add a linear penalty $-m_h|i-j|$ to scores; extrapolates to longer sequences.
- **RoPE (rotary)**: rotate each 2-D pair of $q,k$ by an angle proportional to position: $\langle R_{\theta,m}q,R_{\theta,n}k\rangle$ depends only on $m-n$. Frequencies $\theta_i=10000^{-2i/d}$. Dominant in modern LLMs; context extension by **position interpolation**, **NTK-aware scaling** and **YaRN** (rescale frequencies so a model trained at 4k works at 32k+ after short fine-tuning).

**Three layouts**:
- **Encoder-only (BERT/RoBERTa/DeBERTa)**: bidirectional, trained with masked-LM (15% masking); best for classification/retrieval/embeddings.
- **Decoder-only (GPT/LLaMA/Qwen/Mistral)**: causal LM; dominant for generation and general LLMs; in-context learning emerges with scale.
- **Encoder-decoder (T5/BART/Whisper)**: cross-attention; good for translation/summarisation/speech; span-corruption pretraining.

**Decoding**: greedy, beam search, temperature, top-k, **top-p (nucleus)**, min-p, repetition penalties, **speculative decoding** (small draft model proposes tokens, big model verifies in one pass; exact distribution preserved). Training is parallel over positions (teacher forcing); inference is sequential - hence the **KV cache** (store past K,V: memory $=2\cdot L\cdot n\cdot n_{kv}d_{head}\cdot$bytes).

**Residual stream view**: each block reads from and additively writes to a shared stream; this makes interpretability (circuits, logit lens) tractable and explains why depth-pruning/early exit sometimes works.
tradeoffs: Pre-LN + RMSNorm + SwiGLU + RoPE is the de-facto recipe: stable, efficient, and extendable.
Weight tying saves $Vd$ parameters (large for small models) at slight quality cost for big ones.
pitfalls: Miscounting parameters by forgetting the embedding (dominant in small models) or GQA's smaller K/V.
Using learned positions then trying to run longer than trained.
Applying RoPE to the value vectors (only q,k).
Comparing perplexity across different tokenizers.
interview: Compute the parameter count of a 32-layer, d=4096 transformer.
Why 6ND for training FLOPs?
Explain RoPE and why it extrapolates better than learned positions.
use: Writing the architecture section; budgeting compute; reproducing a LLaMA-style model.
avoid: Do not describe a 'novel architecture' without parameter/FLOP-matched baselines.

qa.q: KV-cache size for LLaMA-7B-like (L=32, 32 heads, d_head=128) at 4k context, fp16, batch 1?
qa.a: $2\cdot32\cdot4096\cdot32\cdot128\cdot2$ bytes $=2.1$ GB per sequence; with GQA (8 KV heads) it is 4x smaller. This is why serving is memory-bound and batch size is limited by KV cache.

title: Efficient attention and long context: FlashAttention, MQA/GQA/MLA, sparse, ring
tagline: How modern models make attention fast and the KV cache small.
explain:
**The bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not FLOPs.** Standard attention writes the $n\times n$ score matrix to GPU HBM (slow) several times. **FlashAttention** tiles $Q,K,V$ into blocks that fit in SRAM and computes softmax *online* with running max/sum so the $n\times n$ matrix is never materialised: exact result, memory $O(n)$, 2-4x faster. FlashAttention-2/3 improve parallelism and use Hopper features/fp8.

**Online softmax**: keep $m=\max$, $\ell=\sum e^{s-m}$ and update when a new block arrives: $m'=\max(m,m_b)$, $\ell'=e^{m-m'}\ell+e^{m_b-m'}\ell_b$, rescaling the partial output accordingly.

**KV-cache reduction** (inference memory $\propto n_{kv}$):
- **MHA**: $h$ K/V heads. **MQA**: 1 shared K/V head (fast, slight quality loss). **GQA**: $g$ groups (e.g. 8) - near MHA quality, 4-8x smaller cache; LLaMA-2/3, Mistral. **MLA** (DeepSeek): compress K,V into a low-rank latent $c=W_{DKV}x$ and up-project on the fly - >90% cache reduction with MHA-level quality.
- **Quantised KV cache** (int8/fp8), **paged attention (vLLM)**: allocate the cache in fixed-size pages to avoid fragmentation, enabling much higher batch throughput; **prefix caching** shares identical prompt prefixes.

**Sparse / local patterns** reduce $O(n^2)$: sliding-window (Mistral, with stacking giving effective receptive field $L\cdot w$), dilated, block-sparse, global tokens (Longformer/BigBird), attention sinks (StreamingLLM keeps first tokens + a window).

**Linear/approximate attention** (Performer, linear transformers, RetNet): replace softmax by a kernel feature map $\phi$ so $\mathrm{Attn}=\phi(Q)(\phi(K)^\top V)$ with $O(n)$ cost and a recurrent form - cheaper but weaker at precise recall. **State-space models** are the other route (next concept).

**Context extension**: RoPE interpolation/YaRN + fine-tuning, long-context data, **ring attention / sequence parallelism** (shard the sequence across GPUs and pass K,V blocks around a ring), chunked prefill. **Lost in the middle**: models use information at the start/end of long contexts better than the middle; evaluate with needle-in-a-haystack, RULER, multi-hop long-context benchmarks - not just perplexity.

**Prefill vs decode**: prefill is compute-bound (parallel over prompt), decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (one token, read all weights + KV) → batching and quantisation help decode most. Use the calculator to see memory budgets.
tradeoffs: GQA/MLA trade a little modelling capacity for a large serving win; choose at pre-training time (converting later needs uptraining).
Sparse attention saves compute but may miss long-range dependencies that full attention captures.
pitfalls: Optimising FLOPs while the kernel is memory-bound.
Evaluating long context with perplexity only.
Window attention without sinks causing quality collapse on streaming.
Quantising the KV cache without checking long-context accuracy.
interview: Explain FlashAttention's tiling and online softmax.
MQA vs GQA vs MLA: what do they reduce?
Why is decoding memory-bound?
use: Serving LLMs, long-document tasks, writing the efficiency section of an architecture paper.
avoid: Do not claim long-context ability from a larger positional limit alone.

qa.a: No - it computes exact softmax attention; only the order of operations (tiling with online normalisation) and memory traffic change, so results match up to floating-point rounding.

title: Mixture of Experts and state-space models (Mamba) - sparse and recurrent alternatives
tagline: More parameters for the same FLOPs, and linear-time sequence mixing.
explain:
**Mixture of Experts (MoE)**: replace the FFN by $E$ expert FFNs and a router. For token $x$: gate $g=\mathrm{softmax}(W_rx)$, pick top-$k$ experts (usually $k=1$-$2$; DeepSeekMoE uses many fine-grained experts + shared experts) and output $y=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{TopK}}g_i\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(x)$ (renormalised). **Total parameters** grow ×$E$ but **active parameters/FLOPs per token** stay near a dense model of size $k\cdot d_{ff}$ — e.g. Mixtral 8×7B: 47B total, ~13B active.

**Load balancing** is essential - otherwise a few experts get all tokens (routing collapse). Switch-Transformer auxiliary loss: $\mathcal L_{aux}=\alpha E\sum_{i=1}^{E}f_iP_i$ where $f_i$ is the fraction of tokens routed to expert $i$ and $P_i$ the mean router probability; alternatives: capacity factors with token dropping, expert-choice routing, auxiliary-loss-free bias balancing (DeepSeek-V3), router z-loss $\frac1T\sum(\log\sum_je^{r_j})^2$ for stability.

**Systems**: **expert parallelism** shards experts across GPUs with all-to-all communication each layer; inference memory holds *all* experts (memory-heavy, compute-light), batches should be large enough to keep experts busy. **Trade-off**: better quality per training/inference FLOP, harder to train/fine-tune/serve (instability, imbalance, communication).

**State-space models (SSMs)**: continuous system $h'(t)=Ah(t)+Bx(t),\ y(t)=Ch(t)$ discretised to $h_t=\bar Ah_{t-1}+\bar Bx_t$, $y_t=Ch_t$. Because it is linear time-invariant it can be computed as a **convolution** during training ($y=x*\bar K$, $\bar K=(C\bar B,C\bar A\bar B,\dots)$ - S4, HiPPO initialisation for long memory) and as an **RNN** with constant memory during inference. **Mamba** makes $\Delta,B,C$ *input-dependent* (selection) - gives content-based filtering - at the cost of losing the convolution form, so it uses a hardware-aware parallel scan. **Mamba-2** shows SSMs ≈ a structured form of (linear) attention. Hybrids (Jamba, Zamba, Griffin/Hawk) interleave SSM/linear layers with a few attention layers for recall + efficiency.

**Where they stand**: SSMs offer $O(n)$ training and constant-memory decoding (great for very long sequences, streaming, audio, genomics) but exact recall/copying and in-context learning still favour attention; pure-attention remains the strongest at scale, hybrids are the pragmatic frontier. Other efficient/recurrent designs to know: **RWKV**, **RetNet**, **xLSTM**, **linear attention with delta rule**.
tradeoffs: MoE: cheap compute/token and high capacity, but large memory footprint and complex routing/parallelism.
SSM: linear time and tiny inference state, weaker at precise retrieval than attention.
pitfalls: Comparing MoE to a dense model on *total* parameters instead of active parameters/FLOPs.
Ignoring routing collapse and not logging expert utilisation.
Claiming SSMs 'replace' attention without recall benchmarks.
Batch size too small at inference for MoE (idle experts).
interview: How does MoE give more parameters at the same FLOPs and what breaks?
Explain the auxiliary load-balancing loss.
Why can Mamba run as both a convolution and an RNN, and what does selection change?
use: Reading frontier-architecture papers; choosing between dense, MoE and hybrid designs.
avoid: Do not pick MoE for small models/small-scale serving where memory is the constraint.

qa.q: Why is MoE memory-heavy at inference even though active params are small?
qa.a: Every expert must be resident (any token may route to it), so memory scales with total parameters, while compute per token scales with active parameters. Throughput gains therefore need large batches and expert parallelism.

title: Tokenisation in depth: BPE, WordPiece, Unigram, byte-level, and their consequences
tagline: Tokenisation silently shapes cost, multilingual fairness, arithmetic ability and many 'model bugs'.
explain:
**Why subwords**: word-level vocabularies explode and cannot handle new words (OOV); characters make sequences long and attention expensive. Subwords balance both.

**BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding)**: start from characters/bytes; repeat: count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent into a new symbol; stop at vocabulary size $V$. Encoding applies merges in learned order. Use the lab to step through merges. **Byte-level BPE** (GPT-2/3/4, LLaMA-3 tiktoken) starts from 256 bytes → no unknown token, handles any text/emoji. **WordPiece** (BERT) picks merges maximising likelihood $\frac{\mathrm{count}(ab)}{\mathrm{count}(a)\mathrm{count}(b)}$, marks continuations with `##`. **Unigram LM** (SentencePiece/T5) starts with a large vocabulary and *prunes* tokens by likelihood loss; supports sampling several segmentations (subword regularisation). **SentencePiece** treats text as raw stream incl. whitespace (language-agnostic).

**Vocabulary size trade-off**: larger $V$ → shorter sequences (cheaper attention, better compression) but bigger embedding/output matrices ($Vd$ params, softmax cost) and rarer tokens that are poorly trained. Typical: 32k (LLaMA-2), 100-128k (GPT-4/LLaMA-3), 256k (Gemma). Compression metric: **bytes or characters per token**; fertility = tokens per word.

**Consequences / pitfalls**
- **Multilingual inequity**: English ≈ 4 chars/token; low-resource languages and code can be 3-10x more tokens → higher cost, shorter effective context, worse quality.
- **Numbers**: inconsistent chunking of digits ("1234" → "123","4") harms arithmetic; fixes: digit-by-digit tokenisation (LLaMA, Gemma).
- **Whitespace/case/glitch tokens**: leading-space variants (`_the` vs `the`), under-trained "glitch" tokens (SolidGoldMagikarp) cause erratic behaviour.
- **Prompt formatting**: special tokens, chat templates, BOS/EOS, trailing spaces change outputs - a common source of eval inconsistency.
- **Cannot easily do character-level tasks** (spelling, reversing, counting letters) because the model never sees characters.
- **Perplexity is not comparable across tokenisers**; use bits-per-byte.

**Beyond tokens**: byte-level models (ByT5, MegaByte, BLT with dynamic patching) and tokenizer-free approaches trade longer sequences for robustness; **vocabulary extension** for new languages requires embedding initialisation (mean of sub-token embeddings) and continued pre-training.

**Training a tokenizer**: use a representative sample of the training mix, normalise (NFKC), pre-tokenise with regex (split digits/punctuation/words), reserve special tokens, evaluate compression per language/domain, freeze it before pre-training.
tradeoffs: Large vocab = shorter sequences and fewer attention FLOPs but bigger embedding/softmax.
Byte-level = robust, no OOV; slightly longer sequences than learned merges.
pitfalls: Comparing perplexity of models with different tokenisers.
Changing the tokenizer after pre-training.
Training on text with different whitespace/normalisation than inference.
Ignoring that a prompt's token count (cost, context) differs by language.
interview: Walk through BPE training on a small corpus.
Why do LLMs struggle to count letters or add large numbers?
How would you add a new language to an existing model?
use: Cost/context estimation, multilingual work, debugging weird generations, writing the data-preparation section.
avoid: Do not hand-write prompt strings without the model's official chat template.

qa.q: Why is bits-per-byte a fairer metric than perplexity across models?
qa.a: Perplexity is per *token* and tokens carry different amounts of text across tokenisers. Converting total log-loss to bits and dividing by the number of UTF-8 *bytes* in the evaluated text gives a tokenizer-independent number.

title: Embeddings: word2vec to contextual and sentence embeddings, similarity and retrieval
tagline: How meaning becomes geometry, how embedding models are trained, and how to evaluate them.
explain:
**Distributional hypothesis**: words in similar contexts have similar meanings. **word2vec** (skip-gram with negative sampling) maximises $\log\sigma(u_o^\top v_c)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb E_{w_k\sim P_n}\log\sigma(-u_{w_k}^\top v_c)$ - implicitly factorising a shifted PMI matrix; **GloVe** fits $w_i^\top\tilde w_j+b_i+\tilde b_j=\log X_{ij}$; **fastText** adds character n-grams (OOV robustness). Static vectors give one vector per word (polysemy problem) and the famous analogies ($king-man+woman\approx queen$).

**Contextual embeddings** (ELMo → BERT → decoder hidden states): the vector depends on the sentence. Layer choice matters (middle layers carry the most semantic info; last layers specialise on the pre-training task). **Anisotropy**: raw contextual vectors occupy a narrow cone so all cosine similarities are high; fix with whitening/centring or contrastive fine-tuning.

**Sentence/text embedding models** (SBERT, E5, BGE, GTE, OpenAI/Cohere/Voyage): encoder (or LLM) trained **contrastively**: positives = (query, relevant passage) pairs, in-batch negatives plus mined **hard negatives**, loss InfoNCE $-\log\frac{e^{s(q,p^+)/\tau}}{e^{s(q,p^+)/\tau}+\sum_je^{s(q,p_j^-)/\tau}}$ with $s=\cos$, $\tau\approx0.02$-$0.05$. Large batches = more negatives. **Matryoshka** training makes the first $m$ dimensions usable alone (truncate for cheaper search). Instruction-prefixed models ("query:" / "passage:") must be used with the right prefix.

**Similarity metrics**: cosine (angle), dot product (needs norm control; used when norms carry meaning), Euclidean (equivalent to cosine on unit vectors: $\|a-b\|^2=2-2\cos$). **ANN search** (HNSW, IVF-PQ, ScaNN) trades recall for latency; quantisation (PQ, binary) shrinks memory 8-32x.

**Evaluation**: **MTEB** (retrieval, STS, classification, clustering, reranking), **BEIR** for zero-shot retrieval, domain-specific held-out sets (public benchmarks are often contaminated/over-fit) with metrics recall@k, MRR, nDCG. **Pitfalls**: domain shift, length bias, embedding drift when the model version changes (must re-index), mixing embeddings from different models.

**Multimodal**: **CLIP** trains image and text encoders with a symmetric InfoNCE over the batch similarity matrix; zero-shot classification = nearest text prompt. **Cross-encoders** (rerankers) score (query, doc) jointly - more accurate but $O(\text{candidates})$ cost; use retrieve-then-rerank.
tradeoffs: Bi-encoders are fast and indexable; cross-encoders are accurate but slow - combine them.
Higher dimension = better recall but more memory/latency; Matryoshka/PQ reduce it.
pitfalls: Using the wrong prefix/instruction or normalisation for a model.
Comparing cosine scores across models (not calibrated).
Not re-embedding after changing the model.
Evaluating on a public benchmark the model was trained on.
interview: How is a sentence-embedding model trained?
Why is cosine on normalised vectors equivalent to Euclidean ranking?
Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder?
use: RAG, semantic search, clustering, dedup, recommendations, classification features.
avoid: Do not use raw LLM hidden states as sentence embeddings without a trained pooling/contrastive step.

qa.q: Why do embedding models need hard negatives?
qa.a: Random in-batch negatives are mostly trivially different, giving near-zero gradient; hard negatives (similar but wrong passages) force the model to learn fine-grained distinctions that matter in retrieval. Beware false negatives in mined hard negatives.

title: Self-supervised learning: masked modelling, contrastive, non-contrastive, multimodal
tagline: How models learn representations from unlabeled data - the engine behind foundation models.
explain:
**Principle**: invent a pretext task whose labels come from the data itself; the representation learned transfers downstream.

**Generative / predictive**
- **Autoregressive LM**: maximise $\sum_t\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t})$ - GPT family; the simplest, most scalable objective; yields general in-context ability.
- **Masked modelling**: BERT masks ~15% tokens and predicts them (bidirectional); T5 span corruption; **MAE** masks 75% of image patches and reconstructs with a light decoder; **BEiT/data2vec** predict discrete tokens or latent targets.
- **Denoising**: diffusion/denoising autoencoders as representation learners.

**Contrastive**: pull positive pairs together, push negatives apart. **SimCLR**: two augmentations of the same image are positives; NT-Xent loss $\ell_{i,j}=-\log\frac{e^{\mathrm{sim}(z_i,z_j)/\tau}}{\sum_{k\ne i}e^{\mathrm{sim}(z_i,z_k)/\tau}}$; needs large batches (or a **MoCo** memory queue + momentum encoder); strong augmentations (crop+colour) are crucial. **CLIP**: image-text pairs, symmetric InfoNCE; 400M pairs → zero-shot transfer. **Alignment & uniformity** (Wang & Isola): good representations align positives and spread uniformly on the sphere.

**Non-contrastive (no negatives)**: **BYOL/SimSiam** use a predictor + stop-gradient; **DINO/DINOv2** self-distillation with centring and sharpening; **VICReg/Barlow Twins** use variance/covariance regularisers. The main danger is **representation collapse** (constant output); it is prevented by negatives, asymmetry (predictor, EMA teacher, stop-grad) or explicit decorrelation.

**Multimodal**: CLIP/SigLIP (sigmoid loss, no global softmax), ALIGN, image-text generative models (Flamingo, LLaVA: vision encoder → projector → LLM), audio (wav2vec 2.0, Whisper), video (VideoMAE).

**Evaluating representations**: **linear probing** (frozen features + linear head), k-NN accuracy, fine-tuning, few-shot, transfer to many tasks. Report probing *and* fine-tuning; they can disagree (MAE is weak at linear probing but strong at fine-tuning).

**Scaling and data**: more diverse data and larger models matter more than the exact objective; data curation (dedup, filtering) is a first-class research variable. **Mutual-information view**: InfoNCE lower-bounds $I(x;y)$ but the bound saturates at $\log N$ and evidence suggests the benefit is not purely MI maximisation.
tradeoffs: Contrastive methods need large batches/negatives; masked modelling and BYOL-style methods avoid them but need collapse safeguards.
Linear-probe accuracy and fine-tuned accuracy rank methods differently.
pitfalls: Collapse: all embeddings identical (monitor feature std and rank).
False negatives in contrastive batches (same class treated as negative).
Augmentations that destroy the information the downstream task needs.
Evaluating only linear probe or only fine-tune.
interview: Why does BYOL not collapse without negatives?
Compare masked modelling and contrastive learning.
What does InfoNCE optimise and what is its limitation?
use: Pre-training on unlabeled data; designing a new self-supervised objective for a domain (medical, remote sensing, time-series).
avoid: Do not claim a better representation without multiple downstream tasks and compute-matched baselines.

qa.q: How do you detect representation collapse?
qa.a: Track the standard deviation of normalised embeddings across a batch (→0 means complete collapse), the rank / singular-value spectrum of the embedding covariance (dimensional collapse), and downstream linear-probe accuracy during training.

title: Graph neural networks: message passing, GCN, GAT, expressiveness
tagline: Deep learning on non-Euclidean data - frequently asked about in applied papers.
explain:
A graph $G=(V,E)$ with node features $X$ and adjacency $A$. A **message-passing** GNN updates each node from its neighbours:

```math
h_v^{(l+1)}=\phi\Big(h_v^{(l)},\ \bigoplus_{u\in\mathcal N(v)}\psi\big(h_u^{(l)},h_v^{(l)},e_{uv}\big)\Big)
```

with a **permutation-invariant** aggregator $\bigoplus$ (sum, mean, max). **GCN** (Kipf & Welling): $H^{(l+1)}=\sigma(\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}H^{(l)}W^{(l)})$ with $\tilde A=A+I$ - a low-pass spectral filter. **GraphSAGE**: sample neighbours and aggregate (scales to large graphs). **GAT**: attention over neighbours $\alpha_{uv}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{LeakyReLU}(a^\top[Wh_u\|Wh_v]))$. **GIN**: $h_v'=\mathrm{MLP}((1+\epsilon)h_v+\sum_uh_u)$ - as expressive as the 1-WL isomorphism test. Transformers are GNNs on fully-connected graphs; **graph transformers** add positional/structural encodings (Laplacian eigenvectors).

**Tasks**: node classification, link prediction, graph classification/regression (molecules), recommendation. **Readout** for graphs: sum/mean/attention pooling over nodes.

**Known issues**: **over-smoothing** (deep GNNs make node features converge; keep 2-4 layers or use residual/jumping knowledge), **over-squashing** (long-range information compressed through bottlenecks), limited expressiveness (1-WL), scalability (neighbour sampling, cluster-GCN), heterophily (neighbours of different classes), **leakage in splits** (transductive vs inductive, test nodes' edges visible during training).

**Where used**: molecules/materials, knowledge graphs, fraud/networks, recommender systems (LightGCN), traffic/time-series, combinatorial optimisation, and as retrieval structure in GraphRAG.
tradeoffs: More layers expand the receptive field but cause over-smoothing; skip connections and sampling mitigate it.
Spectral methods need the fixed graph; spatial methods generalise to unseen graphs.
pitfalls: Information leakage via edges between train and test nodes.
Comparing on tiny citation benchmarks with tuned splits.

qa.q: Why is the GCN normalisation $D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$ used?
qa.a: Plain $AH$ sums neighbour features so high-degree nodes get large magnitudes (scale grows with degree). Symmetric normalisation averages in a degree-aware way, keeps the operator's eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$ and corresponds to a first-order spectral filter on the normalised Laplacian.
